newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota seen hoping to become global telecom player.
newsitem.headline: Toyota seen hoping to become global telecom player.

text.p: Japan's car giant Toyota Motor Corp, seeking to diversify into new, lucrative niches away from its mainstay business, may forge a global alliance in the telecommunications sector, analysts said on Thursday.
"Toyota is likely to pursue alliances with American and European telecommunications firms," Nikko Research senior analyst Noriyuki Matsushima said.
Analysts said Toyota's forays into telecommunications so far have been unsuccessful and it would not be able to survive in that market without some sort of alliance.

But Japan's huge telecommunications market, one of the showcases of Tokyo's deregulation efforts and poised for increased competition from both domestic and foreign firms, is also one of the hottest places for a Japanese company to be.

In March last year, the carmaker took the plunge and formed Toyota Digital Cruise Inc, owned 60 percent by Toyota, to provide telecommunications services, including internet-related services and software development.
Toyota subsidiaries and affiliates Tsusho Corp, Toyotsu Telecommunication Corp and Nippondenso Co Ltd each hold 10 percent stakes. The rest is held by investors.

Toyota already has stakes in 15 Japanese telecommunications service companies including Teleway Japan Corp (TJC) and International Digital Communications Inc (IDC), one of Japan's second-tier international telephone operators, as well as cellular phone operator Nippon Idou Tsushin Corp (IDO).
Toyota owns 36.8 percent of TJC, 17.58 percent of IDC and 27.2 percent of IDO.
On Tuesday, Toyota president Hiroshi Okuda told reporters that his company may be shopping around for a global partner, but stopped short of saying who it might be.
Okuda said the company has already been approached by several foreign companies, including a German firm, on a possible tie-up, although no decision has been made.

"Okuda is a wheeler-dealer," Matsushima said. "It is possible that Toyota will incorporate mergers and acquisitions as part of its diversification strategy, like buying a housing company or other businesses in order to make sure business trends don't get ahead of them."
In addition to telecommunications, Toyota is already dabbling in non-car areas such as housing and marine engines.
In its core car business, Toyota's last year dipped below its long-cherished 40 percent mark in domestic market share for the first time since 1982, falling to 39.1 percent.

But 1996 also brought good news as sales rose 3.7 percent to 2.10 million vehicles, and a Toyota official told Reuters that its domestic market share is sure to reach 40 percent again in its business year to March 1997 in view of current sales conditions.
Meanwhile, the company hopes to make its non-automobile businesses profitable by the year 2000, when Okuda said sales from those businesses would reach one trillion yen, 10 percent of the total.
Currently, Toyota's sales from non-automobile sectors stand at 707 billion yen, about 6.6 percent of overall group sales.

Japan's overall domestic vehicle demand is expected to stall this year after three consecutive years of sales growth. Stiffer competition in the market has made carmakers less optimistic than in the past about sales growth.
